Ribupatide (HRS9531): First Oral GLP-1/GIP Dual Agonist in Phase 3 — Research Dossier

Research compounds discussed for educational purposes. Not FDA-approved for human use where applicable. Consult a healthcare provider before use.

Ribupatide (HRS9531) is a GLP-1 and GIP receptor dual agonist developed by Hengrui Pharma (China) in partnership with Kailera Therapeutics (US). It targets the same two-receptor mechanism as tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound), but is being developed in both injectable (Phase 3 globally) and oral tablet (Phase 2, advancing to Phase 3) formulations. The oral form, if it succeeds in Phase 3, would be the world's first oral GLP-1/GIP dual agonist — combining the efficacy mechanism of tirzepatide with the convenience of a pill.

What is Ribupatide?

Ribupatide is a synthetic peptide that simultaneously activates two incretin hormone receptors: the GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) and the GIP receptor (GIPR). This dual-receptor mechanism is the same underlying pharmacology as tirzepatide. GLP-1 receptor activation reduces appetite and slows gastric emptying; GIP receptor activation is believed to enhance insulin secretion, improve adipocyte insulin sensitivity, and drive thermogenesis in fat tissue. The combination produces greater weight loss than GLP-1 agonism alone.

What makes ribupatide potentially distinctive:

  • Oral formulation in development — the HRS9531 pill would be the first oral GLP-1/GIP dual agonist if it reaches Phase 3 approval
  • Injectable Phase 3 showing 23.6% weight loss at 36 weeks — competitive with the highest numbers seen in Phase 3 obesity trials
  • Developed by Hengrui (a large, established Chinese pharmaceutical company) with global commercialization through Kailera

Mechanism of Action

Ribupatide is a co-agonist of two receptors in the incretin hormone system:

  • GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R): Reduces appetite via hypothalamic signaling, slows gastric emptying, stimulates insulin secretion in a glucose-dependent manner, suppresses glucagon
  • GIP receptor (GIPR): Enhances glucose-stimulated insulin secretion; stimulates adipocyte lipolysis, thermogenesis, and fat mobilization; may improve hypothalamic insulin sensitivity

The dual mechanism is believed to produce additive satiety and metabolic benefits. In preclinical and clinical studies with tirzepatide (the approved GLP-1/GIP dual agonist), the GIP component appears to contribute 30–40% of the total weight-loss effect above GLP-1 alone. Ribupatide's receptor binding profile and pharmacokinetics differ from tirzepatide — whether this translates to different clinical outcomes requires head-to-head data, which does not yet exist.

Key Research Findings

Oral Ribupatide — Phase 2 China (ADA 2026)

Trial: NCT06841445 | Population: N=166 adults with obesity (BMI ≥28 kg/m²) without type 2 diabetes, China | Duration: 26 weeks | Presented at ADA 2026 (American Diabetes Association Scientific Sessions)

  • Weight loss: up to 12.1% mean weight reduction from baseline at week 26 across dose arms (10 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg), vs. 2.3% placebo
  • Responder rate: up to 38.6% of participants achieved ≥15% body weight reduction
  • No plateau: weight loss was still progressing at week 26, suggesting ongoing efficacy potential
  • Safety: consistent with GLP-1-class therapies (nausea predominantly); well tolerated
  • Note: These data have been presented but not yet published in a peer-reviewed journal as of November 2026

Injectable Ribupatide — Phase 3 China

  • 23.6% mean weight loss at 36 weeks in Phase 3 data from China — among the highest figures reported in any obesity Phase 3 trial globally
  • Global Phase 3 for the injectable form is ongoing (Kailera-run)

Next Steps

  • Hengrui plans to advance oral ribupatide to Phase 3 in China
  • Kailera plans to initiate a global Phase 2 for oral ribupatide in 2026, with global Phase 3 targeted for H1 2027
  • Global oral ribupatide mid-stage results expected approximately 2027

Dosing in Research

Oral Phase 2 China data tested multiple doses including 10 mg, 25 mg, and 50 mg once daily (exact dosing frequency — once-daily vs. once-weekly oral — may vary; Kailera has referenced once-weekly oral as the target formulation). Injectable Phase 3 uses once-weekly subcutaneous injection.

Important note: Ribupatide is investigational in both oral and injectable forms outside of China. It is not commercially available in the US, EU, or most markets as of November 2026. This dosing information is provided for scientific context only and does not constitute dosing guidance.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How does ribupatide differ from tirzepatide if both target GLP-1 and GIP?

Both drugs activate GLP-1 and GIP receptors, but are distinct molecular entities from different developers with different receptor binding profiles and pharmacokinetics. The critical differentiator is delivery: ribupatide is in development as an oral pill, while tirzepatide requires weekly injections. Oral GLP-1/GIP dual agonism achieving 12%+ weight loss at 26 weeks (with no plateau) would be unprecedented in the oral obesity drug space. Direct head-to-head trials have not been conducted; any comparison is cross-trial and not definitive.

Q: When might oral ribupatide reach patients?

As of November 2026: oral Phase 2 data from China is positive. Kailera plans a global Phase 2 launch with results expected ~2027, followed by Phase 3 targeted for H1 2027. Standard Phase 3 obesity trials run 52–72 weeks, putting topline results at 2028–2029, and FDA review and potential approval no earlier than 2029–2030. Access is limited to authorized clinical trials in the meantime. The injectable ribupatide may reach certain markets sooner through China's regulatory pathway.

Q: What weight loss did ribupatide achieve and how does it compare?

Oral form (Phase 2 China): up to 12.1% at 26 weeks, still progressing, 38.6% achieved ≥15% reduction. Injectable (Phase 3 China): 23.6% at 36 weeks. For context: oral semaglutide (Rybelsus/OASIS) achieved ~16.6% at 64 weeks; injectable semaglutide (Wegovy) ~14.9% at 68 weeks; tirzepatide (Zepbound) up to ~22.5% at 72 weeks. Oral ribupatide at 12.1% in 26 weeks with no plateau could approach injectable-class efficacy if the trajectory continues — an unprecedented result for an oral weight-loss medication. All comparisons are cross-trial and not head-to-head.

Research Limitations

  • Oral Phase 2 data is from China only (N=166) — not yet peer-reviewed and not yet replicated in a global population
  • 26-week follow-up is shorter than the standard 52–72 weeks used in obesity registrational trials; long-term weight maintenance unknown
  • No head-to-head comparison with tirzepatide or other approved agents
  • Global Phase 2 for oral ribupatide has not yet started; global data expected ~2027
  • Injectable Phase 3 global results pending
  • Oral bioavailability, food effect, and exact dosing regimen details are not yet publicly disclosed for the global formulation
